newsitem.title: VATICAN: Pope beatifies Austrian priests martyred by Nazis.
newsitem.headline: Pope beatifies Austrian priests martyred by Nazis.

text.p: Pope John Paul set two Austrian priests martyred under Hitler on the road to sainthood on Sunday for their refusal "to worship the beast and image" of the Third Reich.

In a beatification ceremony at the Vatican, the Pope said priests Jakob Gapp and Otto Neururer had shown there could be "no compromise between Christianity and the Nazi pagan national socialist ideology".

"They (the priests) sit today on Christ's throne because they refused...to worship the beast and its image," the Pope said, using a line from the Bible's Book of Revelations to compare Adolf Hitler's Third Reich with Satan.
It was the second time this year that the Pope paid such honours to clergymen killed for resisting Nazi rule. In June, he beatified two German priests at a ceremony in Berlin.
During that trip, he also pulled back from defending the Church's cautious policy towards the Nazis by dropping part of a prepared speech.
That policy has embarrassed post-war German Catholics and prompted Jewish criticism the Vatican ignored the Holocaust.

The Pope, himself a victim of Hitler's occupation of his native Poland, praised Gapp for resisting the Nazi annexation of Austria in 1938, which drove the Tyrolean priest into exile in Italy, France and Spain.
Gaap, a Marianist, saw in the "onslaught of the Nazis an apocalyptic event", the Pope said.
Gapp was finally captured in southern France and beheaded by guillotine in Berlin in 1943. He was 46.

The Pope praised Neururer, also Tyrolean, for defending "the sanctity of Chrsitian marriage", a stand for which he was shipped to the Nazi death camps of Dachau and Buchenwald, where he died in 1940 aged 58.
Innsbruck Bishop Reinhold Stecher, who knew Neururer, said he was arrested by the Nazis after advising a girl not to marry a man who had divorced and was leading a dissolute life.
Stecher, in a brief biography of the priest, said the man rejected by the girl "happened to be a personal friend of the 'Gauleiter', that is, the highest Nazi chief in the Tyrol".
The Pope, looked in relatively good shape after the removal of his appendix in October but struggled to control his trembling left hand.
He also put France's Catherine Jarrige a step closer to sainthood through beatification, the penultimate stage before canonisation.
He praised the Dominican sister for sheltering priests during the French Revolution.
